sections.body_en:
Throughout the long years of exile the Land lay desolate, and the few Jews who lived in it did not engage in agriculture. The exiles from Spain, who began to come up to the Land about five hundred years ago, and the Ḥasidim and the disciples of the Gra, who began to come up about two hundred years ago, also hardly engaged in agriculture at all. Only about a hundred and forty years ago did Jews begin to establish agricultural settlements throughout the Land. The first were members of the Old Yishuv in Jerusalem, who went out beyond the walls and, together with new immigrants, set up small footholds, until in the year 5638 they founded Petaḥ Tikva. In 5642 the First Aliya of the 'Ḥovevei Tziyon' began, and through it, by the shemita year of 5649, seven more moshavot arose: Rishon Le-Tziyon, Zikhron Ya'akov, Rosh Pina, Nes Tziyona, Yesud Ha-Ma'ala, Ekron (Mazkeret Batya) and Gedera.

Then the question of resting in Shevi'it arose for the first time, and the problem was twofold, personal and general. Personally, the farmers barely subsisted and needed support, and resting in Shevi'it could bring them to terrible want and the danger of famine. Generally, resting could cause the ruin of the moshavot. For even if some of the farmers could keep hold of their land, it was clear that many would not hold out, and many more Jews of the Diaspora who were thinking of coming up to the Land would refrain from doing so after hearing about the hardships of making a living and the shemita in the Land.

Rav Shmuel Mohilever, one of the Torah giants of the generation and one of the leaders of 'Ḥovevei Tziyon', together with his colleagues Rav Yehoshua of Kutno and Rav Klepfish, head of the beit din of Warsaw, discussed the matter and decided to permit the farmers to remove the fields from the obligation of shemita by selling them to a non-Jew, in such a way that afterwards the Jews would work the fields as hired workers of the non-Jew who owned the field. The famous posek Rabbi Yitzḥak Elḥanan Spektor also supported the heter. And likewise the Sephardi rabbis in the Land, headed by Rav Elyashar, supported the heter, relying on the rulings of the Sephardi rabbis of earlier generations who had lived in the Land.

But the Ashkenazi rabbis in Jerusalem, headed by Rav Shmuel Salant and Rav Diskin, opposed the heter. In their estimation, no great damage was to be expected from resting in Shevi'it, since in any case there were agricultural methods according to which it is good to rest the fields from time to time. They further held that it would be possible to obtain financial support for the upkeep of the settlers who would rest. There were also those who argued that if they were lenient in this, they would be drawn to be lenient in further matters. On the contrary, they feared that precisely the heter would cause the ruin of the moshavot, because it is said in the Torah that exile comes for the sin of neglecting Shevi'it, and conversely, by keeping Shevi'it one merits abundant blessing (Vayikra 25:20-21; 26:34-35, 43; Shabbat 33a; Avot 5:8-9).

In practice, most of the farmers and their supporters felt compelled to rely on the heter, and under the guidance of their rabbis from Europe they turned to the Sephardi rabbis in the Land, who carried out the sale of the fields for them. This too was the position of most of the great rabbis. But there were still many rabbis in the Diaspora and in Jerusalem who opposed it, and the zealots of the generation stood at their side and fought fiercely against the heter and against the rabbis who supported it.

It is worth noting that at first there were among the stringent rabbis also rabbis who felt public responsibility towards the new Yishuv and the farmers, such as the rabbis of Jerusalem. And there were likewise among the stringent rabbis some who enthusiastically supported 'Ḥovevei Tziyon', such as the Netziv of Volozhin and Rav Mordechai Gimpel Yaffe. But from one Shevi'it to the next it became clearer how hard it was for the pioneers to rest, and therefore even among the stringent there were some who changed their view in favour of the heter, as the Aderet testified about himself: in the first two shemitot, while he was in the Diaspora, he inclined to the view of the stringent. But after he came up to serve as rabbi of Jerusalem, he saw the great want, and changed his view to support the heter (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 207). Rav Diskin of Jerusalem too opposed the heter in the first shemita, and in the second shemita, after coming to know the reality, he agreed to the heter in part.

In general, the dispute turned on two axes. The first: whether the heter mekhira is based on the majority of the poskim or on a minority. The second: how pressing the reality is, for it is a well-known rule in halakha that in a pressing situation one may rely even on individual views, and the more severe the pressure, the more correct it is to be lenient.

sections.title_en: 2. Rav Kook and the Heter Mekhira
sections.body_en:
In the year 5664 Rav Kook came up to the Land and began to serve as rabbi of Jaffa and the moshavot, and in the shemita year 5670, twenty-one years after the heter had been introduced by the great rabbis of the previous generation, Rav Kook carried out the heter mekhira.

Over the years that had passed since the beginning of the new settlement, the moshavot had grown and expanded; instead of hundreds of farmers there were already in the Land thousands of farming families who made their living from agriculture. On the one hand this fact made the heter more necessary, and on the other hand it caused its opponents to harden their position, since it had become comprehensive and included many more people and lands.

Another significant change had taken place in the meantime: most of the residents of the first moshavot, members of the First Aliya, were observant of the mitzvot and committed to the rulings of the rabbis. But over the past generation, the accelerated process of secularisation that the Jewish communities in Europe had undergone was reflected in the make-up of the young immigrants who reached the Land in the Second Aliya. So in 5670, many of the new farmers were not fully observant. Most of them were ready to cooperate with the rabbis in matters of Shabbat, orla and the separation of terumot and ma'asrot, but there was no way to persuade them to rest from field work for a whole year. The pioneers' distance from the mitzvot caused the opponents of the heter to intensify their struggle against it and against the rabbis who supported it. And on the other hand, it strengthened the position of those who permitted, who held that through the heter the pioneers would continue to cooperate in matters of kashrut (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 291, 311).

By then the camps had become entirely clear. All the supporters of the new settlement supported the heter. On the other hand, the prominent characteristic of the opponents of the heter was that they had reservations, to one degree or another, about the new Yishuv, and all the more so about the Zionist movement, which had been founded in the meantime, in 5657. Only in the light of this can the harsh opposition to the heter be understood. For as we will learn below, even if in the first generation the stringent rabbis could ignore the view of the lenient, because it was a new issue, in the second generation the stringent already knew the considerations of the heter, and could know that it is far better founded than similar heterim on which it is accepted to rely in a pressing situation, such as eating 'ḥadash' outside the Land. It can only be that the opposition of most of them to the work of settling the Land and to the Zionist movement, many of whose leaders were secular, distorted the straight line of judgement, to the point that they ignored all the firm sources of the heter while gathering every possible argument for stringency. As we will see, the position of those who permitted was weighed and balanced, while they tried to be as stringent as possible in order to keep the mitzva of Shevi'it.

It was not easy for the rabbis who permitted; they had to withstand harsh attacks and slanders from the zealots of the generation. But Rav Kook, who was the rabbi of the moshavot, held his ground and set out the foundations of the heter in his book 'Shabbat Ha-Aretz', and in many responsa and letters. Rav Kook continued to serve as rabbi of Jaffa and the moshavot in the year 5677 too, even though he was not in the Land at the time. After that, in the shemitot of 5684 and 5691, he served as the Chief Rabbi of the Land of Israel. Since for four shemitot Rav Kook was responsible for carrying out the heter, and also set out its foundations in his books, the heter is called by his name.

It can be said that in recent generations there has been no halakhic dispute as great and comprehensive as the dispute over the 'heter mekhira', which includes several great issues: (a) Shevi'it in our time; (b) the law of land of non-Jews; (c) the mitzva of settling the Land and 'lo teḥonem'; (d) discussions about the validity of the sale itself (on the heter today, see below in halakhot 11-14).1

notes_en.en: From the days of Maran Rav Kook onward, a further characteristic began to stand out in the way the issue was presented. Those who permitted tended to act with piety and humility, and out of respect for the view of the stringent presented the two views as equal (as wrote, for example, Rav Tykocinski in Sefer Ha-Shemita and Rav Zevin in 'Le-Or Ha-Halakha'). In this they followed the way of Maran Rav Kook of blessed memory, who acted with exceptional piety. But on the other hand, many of the stringent, from 5670 onward, tended to dismiss the position of those who permitted and to belittle their honour, and even to call them by harsh expressions, such as heretics and uprooters of the Torah and the like, in serious violation of the proper rules of debate between Torah scholars. And since the words of those who permitted rest on the foundations of the Torah and the mitzva of settling the Land, the stringent were dragged in their battle into harming the honour of the Torah, of the great ones of the generation, and of the holiness of settling the Land. It is worth noting that Rav Kook, out of his holiness and piety, tended to stringency in all the mitzvot and halakhot, and only when there was a halakhic necessity to decide would he decide according to the rules of halakha. For example, he wrote in letter 189: "And over this my heart is sick, that we are forced to teach the people to remove the mitzva of Shevi'it." Therefore he always encouraged those who were able to rest. From this some want to learn that he was not at peace with the heter; but when people came out to cast doubt on the heter, he wrote again and again that it is very well founded, and that in truth it would be possible to permit in a pressing situation even without a sale; and he even noted that he did not want to explain all the foundations of the heter, so as not to cause Shevi'it to be forgotten, in the hope that we would soon merit to keep it properly by Torah law. And against those who spread slander about the heter he would protest gently and lovingly, as was his pious way, while firmly defending the farmers, so that their standing would not be harmed, nor the great mitzva they were keeping, the mitzva of settling the Land (see Igrot Ha-Re'aya 192, 241, 253, 310, 312). But this way of his was unique, and usually in similar cases the poskim tended to respond severely to attacks and slanders of the kind spread about Maran Rav Kook. But since Maran the Rav acted with piety, his disciples continued in the line of piety. And since the truth demands redress for the insult done to it, we are obliged not to exaggerate the honour of the opponents of the heter, but to criticise them honestly for not having acted on this issue as has been accepted in Israel for generations.

sections.title_en: 3. The Basis of the Obligation of Shevi'it in Our Time
sections.body_en:
According to most of the poskim, Rishonim and Aḥaronim, the mitzva of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, because by Torah law the mitzvot of the Yovel and Shevi'it must be kept only when all Israel dwell on their land in proper order, each tribe in its place. Therefore, from the time the tribes of Reuven and Gad and half of Menashe were exiled from their inheritance by the king of Assyria, the mitzva lapsed from the Torah. And only when all or most of Israel return to their land, and the Land is again divided among all the tribes of Israel, will the obligation of the Yovel and Shevi'it return by Torah law (above 5:3-4, note 3; below 10:11).

And some of the Aḥaronim hold that the obligation of Shevi'it in our time is from the Torah; and on the other hand there is an important view among the Rishonim that today there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it, because about three hundred years after the destruction of the Second Temple the Great Beit Din, which sanctified months, intercalated years and counted Yovelot, ceased, and from then the obligation of Shevi'it lapsed entirely, and only as a measure of piety did they keep Shevi'it. So is the view of the Razah, the Ra'avad, the Nimukei Yosef and the Meiri, and so one can learn from other Rishonim (above 5, note 5).

In addition, we have already learned (5:7) that the Rishonim also disagreed about the time of Shevi'it. Some say that Shevi'it was in the year 5774 (Rashi and the Rosh), and some say in the year 5772 (the Ra'avad). And although it was accepted in Israel to act according to the view of the Ge'onim, and the year of Shevi'it was 5775, nevertheless we have not left the realm of doubt. And although on the basis of the accepted count we separate ma'aser sheni in the years fixed for it (1, 2, 4, 5), and even say a blessing over its redemption, this does not mean that the views about the doubt over the years are void, for the halakha is that one says a blessing on the basis of custom.

It follows, then, that by the basic law, in a pressing situation it would be possible to instruct the farmers with a full heter, and exempt them entirely from the obligation of resting in Shevi'it. For it is known that when the pressure is very great, even with a mitzva from the Torah, one may rely on the view of an individual who is lenient. All the more so when it is a mitzva whose obligation today, according to most of the poskim, is rabbinic only. All the more so since the one who is lenient and holds that Shevi'it does not apply in our time is not an individual, but this is the view of several of the great Rishonim. All the more so when there is a doubt as to when the seventh year falls. Likewise, one should add to the considerations of the heter the view of Rabbi Yehuda Ha-Nasi, who held, even at a time when it was clear that Shevi'it must be kept by rabbinic law, that because of the pressure the obligation of Shevi'it should be abolished (above 5:5).2

notes_en.en:
It is written in Responsa of the Rashba 1:253, and so wrote the Rema, Ḥoshen Mishpat 25:2, that in a pressing situation, in a matter involving great loss, one relies on the view of an individual. According to the Baḥ and the Taz, Yoreh De'ah 293:4, one relies on the view of an individual even with a Torah mitzva; and so in Ashkenaz they were accustomed to permit the Torah prohibition of ḥadash on the basis of individual views that there is no prohibition of ḥadash outside the Land, or no prohibition of ḥadash in the grain of non-Jews. The Shakh indeed wrote (Yoreh De'ah, Hanhagat Issur Ve-Heter 242) that only with a rabbinic law may one rely on the individual, but with a Torah law there is a Torah obligation to follow the majority, as it is said (Shemot 23:2): "to incline after the many". But Maran the Rav (Introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz, chapter 10) explained that the obligation to follow the majority applies specifically when they sat together and deliberated with one another within the framework of a beit din; and when they did not sit together, it is only by reasoning that it is fitting to follow the majority, and therefore in a pressing situation one relies on the individual even with a Torah law. And so is the view of the poskim in practice. And in Yabi'a Omer, vol. 10, Yoreh De'ah 43, he brought many sources for this from the words of Rishonim and Aḥaronim. All the more so regarding Shevi'it, where even the stringent hold that the prohibition is rabbinic.
Rav Herzog further wrote (Pesakim U-Khetavim 3:48) that the view of those who hold that there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it in our time is not an individual view, but so hold several of the great Rishonim (above 5, note 5), and one may rely on them in a pressing situation and permit work in the fields. And in the Ḥazon Ish 23:4 he argued that in this matter 'the halakha was stated' not according to the view of the Razah. But in this he disagreed with many of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim who took individual views into account in halakha. And even the Rema in Ḥoshen Mishpat 67:1 took into account the view of the Razah, who holds that there is no obligation of Shevi'it in our time. And in Yabi'a Omer, vol. 10, Yoreh De'ah 43, he brought many sources for this from the words of Rishonim and Aḥaronim.
In addition, one should add the doubt about the years (above 5:7), which is a doubt over three years. For it is known that the Second Temple was destroyed at the close of Shevi'it, but they disagreed about the year of the destruction. According to most of the poskim it follows that the year 5775 is Shevi'it, and according to Rashi and the Tur 5774. They further disagreed whether one must count the Yovel, that is, whether every seven shemitot one must add the fiftieth year and only afterwards return to counting shemitot, as brought in the Rambam and as the Ra'avad holds in practice; or whether one should not count the Yovel at all but count the seventh years continuously, according to the view of the Ge'onim and the view of the Rambam in practice (10:4-6). For this reason, according to several poskim one must separate in all the years both ma'aser sheni and ma'aser ani out of doubt, and some even ruled not to say a blessing over the redemption of ma'aser sheni because of the doubt. And although in practice we have a clear custom in the count of the years, and according to it we separate ma'aser sheni in years 1, 2, 4 and 5, and even say a blessing over its redemption, nevertheless the custom does not cancel the doubt, for although one says a blessing on the basis of custom, the doubt remains and joins the view of those who hold that there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it in our time (see above 5, end of note 6). And so wrote in practice, that the doubt about the years is a great foundation for the heter: Simḥa La-Ish, Yoreh De'ah 26, by Rav Elyashar; Otzrot Yosef by Maharei Engel (Shevi'it p. 96); Mishpat Kohen 63. And so wrote at length Yabi'a Omer, vol. 10, Yoreh De'ah 42:8.

sections.title_en: 4. The Law of Fields of Non-Jews
sections.body_en:
The basis of the heter rests on the fact that the law of Shevi'it does not apply to fields owned by non-Jews. This halakha is indeed disputed. Its beginning is in a dispute of Tanna'im and Amora'im, whether the non-Jew's acquisition removes the obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Demai 5:8) it was ruled according to the view of those who hold that the non-Jew's ownership removes the obligation of the mitzvot, and so is the view of some poskim. And from the Babylonian Talmud (Gittin 47a) it is implied that the halakha follows the view of those who hold that the non-Jew's ownership does not remove the obligation of the mitzvot, and so is the view of most of the poskim (above 5, note 11).

But the poskim disagreed about the meaning of the view of those who hold that the non-Jew's ownership does not remove the obligation of the mitzvot. Some say that while the field is in the hands of the non-Jew the mitzvot apply to it (the Mabit); and some say that when the field is in the hands of the non-Jew the mitzvot do not apply to it, but after the non-Jew sells it to a Jew, the obligation of the mitzvot returns to apply to it, without any need to sanctify the land anew for its mitzvot (Rabbi Yosef Karo). So we have a dispute whether the mitzvot dependent on the Land apply in fields of non-Jews (as explained at length above 5:11-12, notes 11-12).

In addition, according to the author of Sefer Ha-Teruma, the view of those who hold that the non-Jew's ownership does not remove the obligation of the mitzvot was said regarding mitzvot whose obligation is from the Torah; but regarding mitzvot whose obligation in our time is rabbinic, such as Shevi'it and terumot and ma'asrot, the non-Jew's ownership removes the obligation of the mitzvot. And so is the view of the Gra (as explained above 5, note 12).

It follows, then, that according to many poskim the non-Jew's acquisition removes the obligation of the mitzva of Shevi'it, and since the mitzva of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, it is clear that the halakha follows the lenient view.

As we learned (in halakha 3), by the basic law, in a pressing situation it is possible to permit Shevi'it entirely on the basis of a combination of two considerations: (a) according to the Rishonim who hold that the obligation of Shevi'it does not apply in our time; although they are a minority, since even according to the stringent Shevi'it is rabbinic, in a pressing situation one may rely on them; (b) the doubt about the date of the seventh year. Therefore, even if there were no possibility of permitting through a sale, there would be no room to protest against those who are lenient on the basis of these views (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 207, 311).

But since there is a possibility of permitting work in the fields through a sale to a non-Jew, which according to many poskim removes the obligation of Shevi'it, the great rabbis ruled to permit the work through the sale to a non-Jew.

By law it would have been possible to permit Jews to do any work in the fields that were sold, including kinds of work written in the Torah, since the obligation of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, and in every dispute the halakha follows the lenient view; therefore there is no need to take into account the view of those who hold that the sale to a non-Jew does not remove the obligation of Shevi'it. And so ruled several of the great rabbis. But most of the rabbis, and Maran Rav Kook, wanted to make a remembrance of Shevi'it, and therefore even after the sale they permitted a Jew to do kinds of work whose prohibition is rabbinic only; but the kinds of work written in the Torah, namely sowing and pruning, reaping, grape harvesting and ploughing, they permitted only through a non-Jew, and only at a time of great pressure did they sometimes permit them to be done by a Jew.

Those who permitted further established that the heter mekhira may be used only for a basic need, such as agriculture, but not for luxuries, such as tending gardens.

Since those who permitted did not want the heter to be fixed for all generations, they established that the heter must be weighed anew every Shevi'it, to examine whether the hour is still pressing and there is a need to make use of it. And Maran Rav Kook would encourage farmers who were able to do so to enhance the mitzva and rest from all work in Shevi'it, on condition that they not spread slander about the heter (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 192, 310, 312).3

notes_en.en:
Something like the heter mekhira was already done about four hundred and fifty years ago, in the year 5327, by Jews who leased fields from non-Jews and employed non-Jewish workers in them, and needed to continue cultivating the fields in Shevi'it; and the Mabit (2:64) and the Mahari"t (Yoreh De'ah 52) ruled that they should rent out the fields to a non-Jew, and so continue to manage the work in the fields. And they ruled to rent them out for two years, so that the seventh year would be absorbed within another year. And Maran Rav Kook explained (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 1, end of se'if katan 1) that by law there is no prohibition in renting for one year, since the non-Jew who rents the field works for himself in order to earn as much as possible from it; but they were stringent to rent it for two years by absorption as an enhancement, so that it would not look like one who asks the non-Jew to work in Shevi'it as his agent. And the Maharam Galanti (Yoreh De'ah 57) was asked in the year 5362 about a field in Lebanon, which is within the borders of those who came up from Egypt, and permitted selling the land to a non-Jew for Shevi'it, because Shevi'it there is rabbinic. Less than two hundred years later, the rabbi of Hebron, R. Mordechai Rubio (died 5543), was asked about a Jew's vineyard, and relied on the Maharam Galanti, and permitted selling the field to a non-Jew for two years by absorption, as explained in his book Responsa Shemen Ha-Mor, Yoreh De'ah 4. And the great Sephardi rabbis followed his approach, headed by the Rishon Le-Tziyon Rav Elyashar, as explained in Responsa Simḥa La-Ish, Yoreh De'ah 26; and it was he who actually arranged the sale in the year 5649, with the agreement of the Rishon Le-Tziyon who preceded him, Rav Panigel. And likewise in 5649 Rav Yitzḥak Elḥanan Spektor, Rav Shmuel Mohilever, Rav Klepfish, head of the beit din of Warsaw, and Rav Yehoshua of Kutno permitted it (Yeshu'ot Malko, Yoreh De'ah 53-57, 59), and so the Avnei Nezer (Yoreh De'ah 458); and so ruled Rav Mordechai Eliasberg, Rav Ḥayim Elazar Wax, Maharei Engel (Otzrot Shevi'it) and the Aderet.
On the other hand, these were stringent: the Netziv (Meshiv Davar 2:56), Rav Soloveitchik in the Beit Ha-Levi (3:1), the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (15:10), Rav Mordechai Gimpel Yaffe. And at first Rav Shmuel Salant and Maharil Diskin inclined to this, and in the shemita of 5656, after they heard of the farmers' distress, they agreed to be lenient with trees. Further, these wrote to be stringent: Divrei Malkiel 7:49; She'elat David, end of part 1. And so wrote the book Beit Ridbaz, and brought letters of agreement to his words from Rav Meir Arik and Rav Ḥayim Berlin. And so wrote Rav Alfandari (Ha-Sava Kadisha 1:22). And there were also other rabbis who joined the proclamations to be stringent.
It must be noted that what most of them had in common, by a decisive majority, was that they did not know the settlers' lives at first hand; most of them lived outside the Land, and were fed on the reports of individuals who regarded the new Yishuv with reservation. And those who knew the settlers, even if at first they inclined to stringency, changed their view to leniency, as the Aderet testified about himself (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 207). And there were also rabbis who, after reading the words of Maran the Rav on the considerations of the heter, saw that they were right, but did not publish their words because of the strife; as the son-in-law of the Maharsham testified, that after the Maharsham read the arguments of Maran the Rav, he retracted and said that his words are true as halakha, but that he did not want to intervene further in the matter because of the quarrelsome.
In practice, those who permitted from the second generation onward were the great rabbis who bore the burden of the public in the Land, headed by Maran Rav Kook, Rav Herzog and Rav Frank, and they gave the reasons for their words in many responsa. And so ruled Rav Uziel and Rav Ovadia Hedaya (Yaskil Avdi 8, Yoreh De'ah 28). And so wrote Rav Tchorsh (Keter Efrayim 3), Rav Tykocinski (Sefer Ha-Shemita), Rav Zevin (Le-Or Ha-Halakha), Rav Kasher (No'am 1, pp. 167-191), Rav Yisraeli (Eretz Ḥemda, part 1, book 1, gate 5), and Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach inclined to this in Ma'adanei Eretz. And so the Chief Rabbis instituted the heter: Rav Unterman, Rav Nissim, Rav Shapira, Rav Ovadia Yosef (Yabi'a Omer, vol. 10, Yoreh De'ah 37-44), Rav Mordechai Eliyahu (Ma'amar Mordechai 21).
Some permitted a Jew to do all the kinds of work, even those whose basis is from the Torah; so is the view of Rav Mohilever, who held that even without a sale one may permit rabbinic kinds of work. And so is the view of the Avnei Nezer, and so it is implied from Rav Elyashar, and so it is testified that Rav Ovadia Yosef ruled orally. But in practice the rabbis who instituted the heter permitted kinds of work whose basis is from the Torah to be done by a non-Jew, and those whose basis is rabbinic by a Jew (see Igrot Ha-Re'aya 198; 310; Yabi'a Omer there 42:6). In the Mishpat Kohen 67 he wrote that even after a sale one should not permit a Jew to harvest grapes and reap. And Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Ma'adanei Eretz, siman 2, wrote that the prohibition of reaping and grape harvesting depends on ownership of the fruit, and if so one may permit a Jew to reap and harvest grapes after the sale.

sections.body_en:
At first sight one should object: it is forbidden to sell land of the Land of Israel to a non-Jew, as it is said (Devarim 7:2): "and you shall not show them favour (lo teḥonem)", which the Sages explained (Avoda Zara 20a): "Do not give them a resting place in the land." And so wrote the Rambam (Idolatry 10:3-4): "One does not sell them houses and fields in the Land of Israel… And why does one not sell to them? Because it is said: 'and you shall not show them favour' – do not give them a resting place in the land, for if they have no land, their dwelling is a temporary dwelling."

But this mitzva was meant to strengthen the dwelling of Israel in the Land, as it is said (Devarim 7:1-2): "When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are going to possess, and casts out many nations before you… and the Lord your God delivers them before you and you strike them, you shall utterly destroy them; you shall make no covenant with them, and you shall not show them favour." If so, when the sale of the land is for a short time and is meant to strengthen Jewish settlement in the Land, there is no prohibition in it at all. As the Aderet wrote, the prohibition was meant to strengthen the hold of Israel on the Land, and it cannot be that because of it our hold should be weakened.4

In addition, even if the sale were not needed to strengthen the settlement of the Land, several poskim wrote that the whole prohibition is a sale in perpetuity, or at least when the non-Jew intends to act there as the owner for some time; and here, when the sale is for a short time with no intention on the non-Jew's part to act as the owner, there is no prohibition of 'lo teḥonem' in it.5

notes_en.en: Many explanations were written on this matter, but for halakha this is the main foundation, and it is brought in the Shemen Ha-Mor, Yoreh De'ah 4; Yeshu'ot Malko, Yoreh De'ah 55, 59; the Aderet in a letter brought at the end of Shabbat Ha-Aretz; Avnei Nezer, Yoreh De'ah 458; Rav Frank (Har Tzvi, Zera'im 2:47); Le-Or Ha-Halakha by Rav Zevin. And so it emerges from the words of the Rambam (Laws of Idolatry 10:3-4, as brought above). And one can learn it from the prohibition of giving a non-Jew a free gift, which is also learned from 'lo teḥonem'; and when giving the gift is for the benefit of Israel, it is permitted to give it to a non-Jew (Ramban and Ran on Gittin 38b). Land is indeed a much greater matter than a gift, and therefore it is forbidden to sell land to a non-Jew for personal benefit; but in order to strengthen the hold of all Israel on the land it is permitted. And not as the Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 24:4, who invented a new definition in this, contrary to the purpose of the mitzva explained explicitly in the Torah.

The Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh (339) wrote that the prohibition is selling in perpetuity. And he added in the name of the Ramban that the prohibition is "to sell to one who will hold it for ever, and this is the non-Jew… and if he stipulated with the non-Jew that he return it, it is permitted to sell it to him." This is brought in the Mishpat Kohen 60. And there is a difficulty from what the Sages forbade, renting land to a non-Jew (Avoda Zara 20b); but the prohibition is when there is harm in this to Israel's hold on the Land, whereas for the sake of strengthening their hold and settling the Land there is no prohibition at all (Mishpat Kohen 63).
In addition, Maran the Rav mentioned in the Introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz, chapter 12, that some say that the main prohibition is selling to a non-Jew who has no land in the Land, for through this he will strengthen his dwelling in the Land, as in the words of the Rambam (Idolatry 10:4). But if he already has land, perhaps there is no prohibition in this, and therefore it is preferable to sell to him. Similarly Rav Frank wrote in Har Tzvi, Zera'im 2:47, on the basis of a responsum of the author of Torat Ḥesed, that it is permitted to exchange land or a house with a non-Jew, for he is not giving him a resting place.
In addition, by Torah law the prohibition of 'lo teḥonem' stems from concern about the bad influence of the non-Jews on Israel, as it is said (Devarim 7:2-4): "…you shall make no covenant with them, and you shall not show them favour. Nor shall you intermarry with them… for he will turn away your son from following Me, and they will serve other gods; and the anger of the Lord will be kindled against you, and He will destroy you quickly." Therefore it is permitted to sell land to a ger toshav, that is, to a non-Jew who has taken upon himself to keep the seven Noahide commandments. But according to the Rambam (Laws of Idolatry 10:6), at a time when the Yovel has lapsed the batei din of Israel may not accept a non-Jew as a ger toshav. But according to the Ra'avad (there 10:6; and Forbidden Relations 14:7), even in our time one who in practice behaves as a ger toshav has the law of a ger toshav, and it is permitted to sell him land in the Land. And although the halakha does not follow the Ra'avad, here, where in any case it is permitted to sell for the reasons mentioned, many wrote that it is preferable to sell to a non-Jew who does not practise idolatry and has the law of a ger toshav. And see the article of Rav Azarya Ariel in 'Ha-Torah ve-Ha-Aretz', vol. 8, p. 391.

sections.body_en:
Some attacked the heter from the other side: that this is not a real sale, since it is clear that the non-Jew does not intend to exercise his purchase, for he understands that this is an act meant for a religious purpose only; and therefore this sale has no validity.

But there is nothing in this argument, because by halakha, if a legal sale was made, the land does in fact belong to the non-Jew, and consequently the laws of Shevi'it do not apply to it. And so we find in many halakhot that, when needed, a legal act of sale is carried out in order to be exempt from a mitzva that is hard to keep.

For example, it is a mitzva from the Torah to give the firstborn of pure animals to the kohen, and the kohen must offer them as sacrifices in the Temple and eat their meat in purity. And today, when the Temple is destroyed, the firstborn of the animal remains in its holiness without the kohen being able to do anything with it. And the Sages ruled to sell to a non-Jew the gullet and windpipe of all the animals about to give birth for the first time, and since the non-Jew is a partner in the animal, the firstborn it bears will not be holy, and they can treat it like other animals. Here too it is clear that this sale has no practical meaning, and even after they slaughter the animal they will not call the non-Jew to come and take his windpipe and gullet, for they have no value; but in practice, since they made a kinyan and the windpipe and gullet legally belong to the non-Jew, the non-Jew becomes a partner in the animal and there is no longer holiness in the firstborn it bears (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 320:6).

And the law of the firstborn is more severe, for the prohibition of eating the meat of a firstborn is from the Torah, whereas the prohibition of Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic. And if regarding the severity of the law of the firstborn one relies on a legal sale, all the more so one should rely on a sale for the purpose of removing the law of Shevi'it.

And likewise regarding the law of ḥametz on Pesaḥ: whoever keeps ḥametz in his possession transgresses two Torah prohibitions, 'it shall not be seen' and 'it shall not be found', and when needed it is permitted to sell the ḥametz to a non-Jew in order to be exempt from these prohibitions, even though the chance that the non-Jew will use the ḥametz he bought is slight. And so we find in further halakhot that the Sages established making use of a kinyan whose whole purpose is to exempt a person from a certain halakhic obligation; so there is nothing in the argument of the opponents of the heter.6

notes_en.en: The law of the sale of ḥametz is explained in Peninei Halakha, Pesaḥ chapter 6. And likewise the Torah commands that one who redeems ma'aser sheni add a fifth, and when needed, in order to be exempt from adding the fifth, they permitted him to give money to his fellow so that he would redeem his fruit, and afterwards return it to the first owner (Mishna Ma'aser Sheni 4:4). And likewise if Reuven forbade Shimon by vow from benefiting from his property, and Shimon has nothing to eat and Reuven wants to help him, the Sages ruled that Reuven should give food as a gift to Levi, and Levi should give it to Shimon, and in this way Reuven does not transgress his vow, for Shimon does not benefit from his property but from Levi's property (Nedarim 48a). And likewise one who did not set an eruv tavshilin may not cook on Yom Tov for Shabbat, and when needed they permitted him to transfer his food to his fellow, so that his fellow would cook it and afterwards give it to him (Beitza 17a). One should add that the heter mekhira is like the heter of the prozbul explained in the previous chapter.

sections.body_en:
The stringent further argued that the sale has no legal validity, since it is not carried out according to the accepted rules of sale with registration in the Land Registry. As was ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (Ḥoshen Mishpat 190:7), in a place where it is customary to write a document for the kinyan, as long as they have not written a document the sale is not complete. If so, in a place where it is customary to register the sale of land in the Land Registry, if it was not registered it has no validity (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan there, 25). Not only that, but one must do so because it is the law of the kingdom (Shulḥan Arukh, Ḥoshen Mishpat 194:2).

But this argument is rejected, because all the discussions about whether a certain kinyan takes effect or not are when there is an argument between the seller, who claims that the sale has no validity, and the buyer, who claims that it has validity; and then one must clarify whether the seller made a final decision to sell. But here, where the seller and the buyer want it to have validity, without any doubt the sale takes effect (Yabi'a Omer, vol. 10, Yoreh De'ah 40). Further, if they write explicitly that no claim will be considered against this sale, as is customary in deeds of sale, the kinyan takes effect even if it was done not in the accepted way (Kiddushin 26a). So this sale is a legal sale; not fictitious, and also not for the buyer to use the field, but a sale for the purpose of a legal definition, that the buyer is the owner for the duration of the seventh year; and as such both sides want it to stand, and make a final decision to agree to all that is needed for it to stand. And so it has been practised regarding the sale of ḥametz: even in places where the law requires registering every sale for tax purposes, since both sides agreed to it, the sale of ḥametz has validity even without registration as required by the law of the king or the state. Even so, since the opponents persisted in attacking the heter unjustly, at the initiative of the Chief Rabbi of Israel, Shlomo Goren of blessed memory, the Knesset passed a law in the year 5739 according to which the sale of land in Shevi'it by the Chief Rabbinate is valid even without paying a fee and registering in the Land Registry.

The author of the 'Ḥazon Ish' further argued against the sale that, since it is forbidden to sell land to a non-Jew in the Land of Israel because of 'lo teḥonem', when the farmers appoint the rabbis as their agents to sell the land, the rabbis become agents for a transgression, and their acts have no validity, for their agency is void, "for there is no agent for a transgression" (Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 24:4). But those who do so act according to great rabbis who hold that it is permitted, and therefore they are not considered agents for a transgression, and their agency has validity. Beyond this, his argument does enormous harm to the great rabbis of the Land: not only did he disagree with them, when they were the rabbis of the place and greater than he in wisdom, in responsibility and in understanding of the reality, but he went further and argued that their view does not count at all, to the point that those who act like them are considered transgressors.7

notes_en.en: To our great sorrow, in the wake of such severe and harsh positions against the great rabbis, for three generations already many of the rabbis of the Ḥaredi public have been afraid to clarify the great issues properly, out of fear that if they express a position not to the liking of the zealots, all their views will be disqualified, and they will be denounced and cast out of the camp as inciters and seducers to transgression. So it happened that in several matters the Ḥaredi public strayed from the way of the Torah, to the point that many of its members became accustomed to scorn great rabbis, such as Maran Rav Kook and his disciples, even though in private many of their own great rabbis oppose this. So it also happened that many became accustomed to set aside the mitzva of settling the Land, of which the Sages said that it is equal to all the mitzvot; and many dare to deny publicly the great mitzva kept by the soldiers who defend the people and the Land. They even invented new prohibitions against secular studies and national service, and other various stringencies that depart from the line of halakha. And against all these things there are many Ḥaredi rabbis who are opposed in private, but they do not state their view openly out of fear of being harmed by the men of strife. And regarding the Ḥazon Ish himself one can offer a little merit: he was very firm in character, and whatever arose in his learning he wrote without deferring to those greater than he. And one can likewise offer this merit regarding the Ridbaz, who was sharp and stormy, and the fervour of Torah overcame him, and at times he expressed sorrow at having come to scorn Maran Rav Kook. But it is hard to offer this merit regarding all those Ḥaredi rabbis who were of ordinary character, and nevertheless dismissed entirely the view of the great rabbis. And certainly one cannot offer this merit regarding those who further added words of disparagement and contempt against the authors of the heter, who were greater and more righteous than they.

sections.title_en: 9. Why They Did Not Permit This in the Past
sections.body_en:
After all that we have learned, there is room to ask why they did not use this heter in the years after the destruction of the Second Temple, in which Israel had great difficulty keeping Shevi'it. For in addition to the great difficulty of any farmer in getting by while resting from the work of his field for a whole year, the Romans also imposed heavy taxes on Israel, which they had to pay in the seventh year as well.

About the days in which Israel was obliged in Shevi'it from the Torah there is no question, for it is clear that there is no room to look for ways to evade the mitzvot of the Torah, especially since the Torah itself promised that by virtue of keeping the mitzva Israel would endure on their land with blessing, and if, God forbid, they neglect the shemita, they will be exiled from their land. Nor is there a question about the days of the Second Temple, in which they were obliged by rabbinic law, since for these very days the Sages instituted keeping Shevi'it, in the hope that their settlement would become established until all the exiles returned to their place and Shevi'it again applied by Torah law. But about the days after the destruction there is a question.

A first answer: indeed Rabbi Yehuda Ha-Nasi, the head of the Sages of Israel, wanted to abolish the mitzva of Shevi'it entirely. But for such a decision he needed the agreement of all the Sages of his generation, and since Rabbi Pinḥas ben Yair did not agree to it, he held back from putting his idea into effect (Yerushalmi Demai 1:3; Ta'anit 3:1; above 5:5).

My teacher and master Rav Avraham Shapira of blessed memory further explained that since in those days the ruling Romans and the non-Jews living in the Land tried to uproot Israel from their fields, there was no possibility of carrying out any kind of sale, lest the enemies of Israel exploit it to dispossess the Jewish seller of his land.

One must further say that in the time of the Sages there was no doubt as to when Shevi'it fell, and according to all views they were obliged to keep Shevi'it by rabbinic law; therefore they did not try to exempt themselves from the mitzva. But since the beit din that sanctified months and counted Yovelot ceased, some hold that there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it, and a doubt has even arisen regarding the date of the seventh year, so that even without a sale it would have been possible to be lenient in a pressing situation; all the more so with the addition of a sale (see Introduction to Shabbat Ha-Aretz 14).

Maran Rav Kook of blessed memory further explained that at a time when most of the land was in the hands of Israel, there was a decree on Israel not to work even in fields of non-Jews, because of appearance, and lest they come through this to work in fields of Israel. But after most of the land was in the hands of non-Jews, the decree lapsed, and the decree should not be renewed without a new decision of the Sages (Shabbat Ha-Aretz, Kuntres Aḥaron 20). And today too, when most of the land is in the hands of Israel, since most of the farmers make use of the 'heter mekhira', there is no room to bring back the decree (Kerem Tziyon 19, Gidulei Tziyon 4; Yabi'a Omer, vol. 10, Yoreh De'ah 42:6).8

notes_en.en: See above 5, note 12, that some Rishonim hold that the halakha does not follow the view of Rav that a Jew may not work in a non-Jew's field. And some hold that the prohibition is only when Shevi'it is from the Torah, and according to their views there is no question at all. But some hold that the prohibition of working in a non-Jew's field applies even when Shevi'it is rabbinic, and above the words of Maran the Rav were brought in resolving this view. And in the Aseh Lekha Rav 5:50 he further wrote that since the First Temple was destroyed for the sin of Shevi'it, when they returned in the days of the Second Temple they were very careful to keep Shevi'it with self-sacrifice. But now there is no longer reason to be concerned about Shevi'it in particular, and one follows the rules of halakha.

sections.body_en:
As we have already learned, at the first stage there were among the opponents of the heter rabbis who supported 'Ḥovevei Tziyon'. But at the second stage the camps became clear, with the opponents of the heter also opposing the Zionist movement, which arose in the year 5657 and began to lead the mitzva of settling the Land. It is important to understand this connection, because according to the rules of ruling, the 'heter mekhira' is properly founded; and not only that, but it leans to stringency compared with what is accepted in similar cases of pressure (as explained in halakhot 3-5). But if one holds that there is no point in settling the Land without resting in Shevi'it, and also that there is no virtue in keeping the mitzva of settling the Land through Jews who are not careful about the mitzvot, there is no need to find a heter to work in Shevi'it.

But the heter is based on the mitzva by which the Torah commanded Israel to settle the Land, and all Israel are commanded in it, both those who are careful about the mitzvot and those who are less careful. And since resting in Shevi'it could harm the keeping of the mitzva of which the Sages said that it is equal to all the mitzvot (Sifrei Re'eh 53), it is fitting to remove the mitzva of Shevi'it, whose obligation in our time is rabbinic, by selling the fields to a non-Jew. For even without resting in Shevi'it the difficulties of aliya and settlement were enormous, and only a few agreed to come up to the Land; all the more so would the immigrants and settlers become fewer if they had to rest from work in Shevi'it. Therefore the rabbis held that it is fitting to find a heter in order to help as many Jews as possible come up to the Land and become established in it and take hold of as much land as possible. In time it became clear that the necessity was far graver, because many of those who remained in the European exile were murdered by the Nazis or were trapped under the persecuting Communist regime.

The opponents further argued that the Torah had already addressed the question of the pressure of the shemita, and instructed us to rely on the blessing of God, as it is said (Vayikra 25:20-22): "And if you say, What shall we eat in the seventh year? Behold, we shall not sow nor gather in our produce. Then I will command My blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth produce for the three years. And you shall sow in the eighth year, and eat of the old produce until the ninth year; until its produce comes in you shall eat the old." But the poskim have already written that this blessing is promised at a time when the mitzva of Shevi'it applies by Torah law, but when the mitzva is rabbinic this blessing is not fulfilled.9

From here we come to a further consideration. Some of the opponents held that one must rely on God to gather Israel in, settle them on their land and sustain them. And if one already comes up to the Land, one must keep Shevi'it and rely on God to help those who rest to get by. So their whole approach is to rely on a miracle. But the Sages of Israel throughout the generations ruled that Israel must plan their way according to reason and not rely on a miracle (Shabbat 32a). Not only that, but it is forbidden to test God whether He will help us by virtue of our keeping His mitzvot, as it is said (Devarim 6:16): "You shall not test the Lord your God, as you tested Him at Massa" (Ta'anit 9a). Therefore the great ones of Israel roused the public to come up to the Land, to settle its soil, and to bring the redemption closer by natural means. And likewise regarding Shevi'it: if one sees that in practice resting in Shevi'it, whose obligation is rabbinic or a custom of piety, will hold back the settlement of the Land, one must make use of the 'heter mekhira' in order to keep the great mitzva of settling the Land by strengthening aliya and settlement.

And there are some of the stringent, who were not community rabbis, whose basic position was that one must always be stringent in order to satisfy all the views, and therefore they opposed a heter that is not according to all the poskim. But the great ones of Torah never acted so, and did not impose stringencies on the public, but preferred to follow the ways of permission, as the Gemara says: "the power of permission is preferable." All the more so in a matter that the public cannot bear, in which the great ones of Israel took the trouble to find a heter in order to save Israel from sin. Not only that, but the tendency to be stringent with the public on the basis of a minority of the poskim and beyond what the law requires sets aside the rules of halakha and presents the Torah in a distorted way (Oraḥ Mishpat 112; Igrot Ha-Re'aya 189).

Furthermore, Maran Rav Kook of blessed memory wrote that one cannot estimate the magnitude of the desecration of God's Name and the destruction of the Torah that could be caused if they are stringent in this beyond what is required, for by this they strengthen the heretics who argue that the Torah does not enable Israel to survive, and therefore one must shake off its mitzvot (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 291, 311).

notes_en.en: So wrote the Sma, Ḥoshen Mishpat 67:2; the glosses of the Ya'avetz and the Ḥatam Sofer on Gittin 36a; the Pe'at Ha-Shulḥan (29:3), Yeshu'ot Malko, Yoreh De'ah 53, Maharei Engel in Otzrot Yosef p. 102; Maran Rav Kook (letter 555) and others. And not as the words of the Ḥiddushei Ha-Rim on Gittin there, and the Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 18:4. And in general we have learned that the conduct of the Land of Israel is in a natural way, and therefore the manna ceased when they entered the Land; as Maran the Rav wrote: "The holiness that is in nature is the holiness of the Land of Israel, and the Shekhina that went down into exile with Israel is the capacity to establish holiness in opposition to nature. But the holiness that fights against nature is not a complete holiness" (Orot Ha-Teḥiya 28). So the main sanctification of God's Name and the blessing in the Land of Israel are by way of nature. It is further explained in the Yerushalmi, Ma'aser Sheni 4:3, that from what is said (Devarim 14:24): "for the Lord your God will bless you", the Sages learned that when needed it is permitted to use a circumvention in the redemption of ma'aser sheni through a fellow, in order to be exempt from adding the fifth. So the Sages learned that we must make an effort so that the blessing that God promised us reaches us, and this effort sometimes includes even a circumvention in order to remove the obligation of the mitzva. And presumably this is required in a state of national spiritual weakness, as in the time of the Second Temple, when the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot was according to most of the poskim rabbinic (above 5:4; below 11, note 2).

sections.body_en:
As we learned (in halakha 5), every Shevi'it one must examine whether we are still in a pressing situation that requires us to use the 'heter mekhira'. By the kindness of God, our situation today is incomparably better than that of the first immigrants, who suffered terrible want. From then until today the Jewish settlement in the Land has gradually become established. Even before the founding of the State there were shemitot in which there was no longer a danger of famine for the settlers, but there was still a great need for the heter, because resting would have brought the settlers down into poverty and harmed the momentum of settlement and the absorption of immigrants. In the first shemitot after the founding of the State too, when many still made their living from agriculture, resting in Shevi'it could have harmed the existence and security of the State, which needed every possible financial resource in order to continue absorbing immigration, building the Israel Defence Forces, and establishing the State of Israel against its enemies.

But in recent shemitot our situation has greatly improved. The State of Israel is already considered a rich and developed country. Thanks to scientific developments and new machines, few people today produce a great yield. From a situation in which most of the Yishuv made its living from agriculture, we have reached a situation in which only about 1.5% of the population makes its living from agriculture. The economic weight of agriculture has also fallen, and today it stands at only about 2% of national output.

At first sight one could argue that in such a situation it is no longer right to use the heter; but on the other hand, the regrettable fact that most of the public does not keep the mitzvot properly greatly affects our situation. Let us examine the issue from three sides: (a) the individual farmer; (b) responsibility for the public as a whole; (c) the State as a whole.

sections.title_en: 12. The First Aspect: The Individual Farmer
sections.body_en:
The individual farmer who wants to keep Shevi'it must compete with farmers who do not keep Shevi'it. And since today a farmer's infrastructure costs are very high, in order to cover these costs in six years as against his competitors' seven, he will have to raise the prices of his produce during the six years. In addition, he must support himself and his family and save for a pension through six years of work, as against his competitors, who do so in seven years. If he wants to live at the accepted standard, he will have to raise the prices of his produce further during the six years. But if the prices of his produce are high, buyers will prefer his competitors. If he sells at their prices, his investments and his work may no longer pay. The clear measure of this is to put the question to the farmers: what will they do if they have to rest in the seventh year? Today most of them think that, having no choice, they would have to change profession. If so, it is clear that their personal situation is one of a pressing situation, and they may use the 'heter mekhira'.

That is to say, one does not measure the farmers' standard of living today against their standard a hundred and thirty years ago, when the heter was established, but against the standard of living accepted today. And if farmers today would reach a state of pressure that would force them to look for other work, that is a sign that they are in a pressing situation, and it is fitting for them from the outset to use the heter. And there is nothing to argue against them; rather, they should be praised for meriting to hold on to the land, to grow the holy fruit of the Land of Israel, and to keep the mitzva of settling the Land, which is equal to all the mitzvot. And it is a mitzva to remove, through the sale, the mitzva of Shevi'it, which applies in our time by rabbinic law, and some say as a measure of piety, in order to keep the mitzva of settling the Land and to widen the borders of Israeli farmers. Indeed, one who is able to rest in Shevi'it, 'holy' shall be said of him, and we must encourage him in this, and even work to allocate state budgets for those who rest in Shevi'it, as will be explained below (11:1).

sections.title_en: 13. The Second Aspect: Responsibility for the Public as a Whole
sections.body_en:
Since most of the farmers are traditional or secular, there is no chance that they will obey a demand to rest in Shevi'it. However, since the great majority of them respect the tradition, if they are offered to sell the fields in order to remove the obligation of Shevi'it, they will do so willingly. And since this is so, this is a pressing situation, and it is fitting for the rabbis to encourage them to sell their fields in Shevi'it, in order to save them from sin.

In addition, if they do not sell the fields, the fruit that grows in them will be holy with the holiness of Shevi'it, and it will be distributed throughout the Land, while the traditional and secular public stumbles and transgresses with it the prohibition of trade and a lack of care with the holiness of the fruit of Shevi'it, and at times, unawares, religious people too may stumble in this. Again this is a pressing situation, for in our public situation, in which those careful about the mitzvot are a minority, there is no possibility of preventing the distribution of this holy fruit, and it is fitting for the rabbis to carry out the sale, in order to remove the fruit growing in them from the holiness of Shevi'it, so that the broad public not sin through it.

Furthermore, if in the seventh year fruit of Shevi'it is distributed without supervision and contrary to halakha, the national kashrut system could be breached for the whole seven years.

sections.title_en: 14. The Third Aspect: The State as a Whole
sections.body_en:
Although agriculture's share of national output is only about two percent, since this is a state, it amounts to enormous sums. That is to say, if the State wanted to finance resting in Shevi'it, it would need to invest about ten billion shekels in it, partly as compensation for the farmers who rest, and partly to cover the deficit in the State treasury arising from the loss of the farmers' taxes. Such a cut in the State budget is equivalent to a pressing situation. Indeed, in difficult years the State of Israel is forced to make such cuts, and even larger ones, in its budget; but these cuts are painful and hard, and they are spread across all the government ministries, including areas in which cutting borders on danger to life: for example, postponing the expansion of hospitals to admit patients, postponing the building of additional operating theatres, delaying the paving of roads, delaying the acquisition of sophisticated weapons, postponing the establishment of additional police units to deal with crime. The cut could also require a reduction in allowances for children, the poor and the elderly, or at the very least delay increases that were planned in these budgets. The cut would also harm the education system, and would include a cut of at least hundreds of millions of shekels in the budget of the yeshivot. And with the present make-up of the population it seems that the cut in the budget of the yeshivot and of the religious and Ḥaredi education systems would be much greater, for one must estimate that if the representatives of the religious and Ḥaredi public demand that the State finance resting in Shevi'it, the representatives of the secular and traditional public will demand that the main cut be in areas that concern the religious and Ḥaredi public. It seems that in such a situation the great rabbis would decide that it is better not to raise the sword of cuts and harm many activities, all of them mitzvot from the Torah, in order to enhance the keeping of a mitzva whose force today is rabbinic, and some say a measure of piety, and which can be removed through the 'heter mekhira'.

Indeed, in the long term, the good economic situation of the State of Israel enables us to plan the way to full rest in Shevi'it, as will be explained below (11:1).

sections.title_en: 15. Those Who Ban the Fruit of the Heter
sections.body_en:
Some argue that it is forbidden to eat fruit grown within the framework of the 'heter mekhira', but their words are contrary to the rules of halakha, and are based on the sin of scorning Torah scholars of the most severe degree. For we learned (above 3:8) that even when the fruit was grown and tended through outright prohibitions, according to most of the poskim it is permitted to be eaten. And although there are some who disagree and forbid the fruit, since the view of most of the poskim is to be lenient, and in addition Shevi'it in our time is rabbinic, the halakha follows the words of the lenient. So the stringent rule contrary to the rules of halakha. All the more so when the farmers are not working through a prohibition but according to the ruling of great rabbis; therefore there is no room at all to argue that the fruit will be forbidden.

Some indeed argue that regarding field crops there is a special prohibition, for the Sages decreed that aftergrowths that grew by themselves are forbidden to be eaten; all the more so is it forbidden to eat vegetables grown through a prohibition. But all this would be correct if the farmers sowed without a heter; but once they sow according to the ruling of the rabbis, there is no prohibition in eating the vegetables. And even those who disagree with the 'heter mekhira' must admit this, since the whole decree on aftergrowths is rabbinic, in order to prevent a prohibition, and consequently where the farmers acted according to the ruling of the rabbis there is no room to forbid. All the more so in our time, when some hold that there is no obligation to keep Shevi'it, and there is a dispute about when the seventh year falls (above halakha 3; above 5, note 5; 5:7).

And some argue that just as it is forbidden to buy fruit from those suspected of working in Shevi'it, so as not to assist a transgression, so it is forbidden to buy fruit grown within the framework of the 'heter mekhira'. But since the farmers work according to the heter of the rabbis, there is no transgression at all in their acts. And those who argue that it is forbidden to assist them entirely dismiss the words of the rabbis who permit, and transgress the severe prohibition of scorning Torah scholars and creating strife.

So those who hold that it is forbidden to eat fruit of the heter mekhira pile reasoning upon reasoning for stringency, against the rules of halakha. In addition, they harm the honour of the great ones of Israel who ruled for the heter according to the words of most of the poskim, in order to help the holy people of Israel returning to their land. This argument is not directed against those who studied the issue and reached the conclusion that it was not fitting to use the 'heter mekhira', and therefore prefer to refrain from eating fruit of the 'heter mekhira', on condition that they act so for themselves as a custom of piety, and instruct the public that by law it is permitted to eat fruit of the 'heter mekhira'. This argument is directed against those who argue that the fruit of the heter is forbidden to be eaten by all, and that one should not eat at the home of someone who relies on the 'heter mekhira', and should not rely on kashrut supervisions that rely on the 'heter mekhira'; for they sin by scorning the great ones of Israel, and raise a hand to harm the holiness of all Israel and of the Land of Israel. And whoever lends a hand to this ban is a partner in their sin.10

notes_en.en: Regarding those who ban, see Minḥat Yitzḥak 8:96. In the Or Le-Tziyon, in the introduction to Shevi'it, he forbade vegetables that are aftergrowths. And see Minḥat Shlomo 1:44, who wrote that even the stringent, after they have ruled that in their view the fruit is forbidden to be eaten, if they are asked for halakha in practice, must rule that in a doubt about the words of the Sages the halakha follows the view of the lenient, and therefore they are not able to forbid the fruit that grew under the heter mekhira. Similarly he wrote in the Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:186, and similar to this Even Ha-Ezer 4:61:2. And similarly in Hilkhot Shevi'it by Rav Zilber 9:62. And the source for this is in Responsa of the Mabit 1:21. And see Ma'amar Mordechai 18:16. Similarly we learned regarding the prohibition of benefiting from work done on Shabbat, that as long as there is a dispute whether the thing is forbidden, there is no prohibition in benefiting from it (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 318:2; Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 26:5). And worked produce is forbidden because of a penalty, so one can learn from Shabbat that one should not penalise where there is a dispute. And all the more so one should not forbid because of aftergrowths when the farmers did so according to the ruling of the rabbis.
